text: Rinsing your hands with plain water barely cleans them. Add soap, and grease and germs get pulled right off. How can a slippery bar do that?
A soap molecule is shaped like a tadpole. Its head loves water. Its tail hates water, and loves grease.
Grease and dirt hold germs onto your skin, and plain water slides right past. But soap's tails dive into the grease, while the heads stay in the water.
Scrub, and the tails wrap around the grease, forming tiny balls called micelles, with the heads facing out. Now water can carry the whole ball away.
Quick test. How long should you scrub with soap? A, five seconds. B, twenty seconds. Or C, two minutes? Think!
Twenty seconds, about two rounds of happy birthday. Soap needs time, and friction, to get under the grease and lift it.
Some viruses, including flu and coronaviruses, wear a fatty coat. Soap's tails dig into it and tear the virus apart.
Two tips. Don't skip your thumbs, your fingertips, and between your fingers, where dirt hides. And water temperature barely matters, so use whatever is comfortable.
Watch again, and count the micelles.
